passage: Saturday: At lunch Madhav's grandfather Shankar pushed his rice around the plate. "You children never talk to me now. Only the phone." Madhav felt a hot flush of guilt and stared at his screen, glued to the corner. Sunday: In the evening Madhav put his phone in the drawer in the hall. "Dada, will you tell me a story?" Shankar's eyebrows shot up. He told about walking to school through mustard fields in bare feet. Madhav asked how far and whether there were snakes. The following Saturday: Shankar was waiting on the veranda with two cups of milk. "Story time?" he asked. Madhav grinned and ran to leave the phone inside.

qa.q: What did Shankar say the children did instead of talking to him?
qa.a: He said they only had the phone.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when his grandfather said the children never talk to him?
qa.a: Guilt; he felt a hot flush and stared at his screen.

qa.q: What did Madhav do that gave both of them something they needed?
qa.a: He put the phone away in the drawer and asked his grandfather for a story, which gave Shankar company and Madhav a good talk.

qa.q: What might Shankar have felt when Madhav asked for a story?
qa.a: Surprise and probably gladness, since his eyebrows shot up and the next Saturday he was waiting with milk.

grounding: A child feels guilty when his grandfather says phones keep the children from talking, then sets the phone aside for story time across days.

passage:
In the clinic waiting room, Pola sat between Tenzin and Aditi, waiting for his eye check-up. Both children were bent over their phones. Twenty minutes passed.
Pola sighed and spoke to no one in particular. "When I was young, grandchildren sat at their grandfather's feet. Now they sit next to him and are somewhere else."
Tenzin's thumb stopped. His ears went warm. He looked at Pola's hands, folded on his walking stick, and felt a lump of guilt.
He slid the phone into his pocket and nudged Aditi, who did the same.
"Pola, tell us about crossing the mountains again? The part with the yak."
Pola's face creased into a smile. By the time the nurse called his name, the yak story had grown three new bits, and Aditi was holding his hand.

qa.q: Why were they waiting at the clinic?
What did Tenzin feel when Pola sighed?
qa.a: He felt guilty; his ears went warm as he looked at Pola's folded hands.

qa.q: What small step turned the wait around?
qa.a: Putting the phones away and asking Pola for the yak story.

qa.q: How did Pola feel before and after the phones were put away?
qa.a: At first he felt lonely and disappointed, then happy, smiling and adding new bits to his story.

grounding: A boy feels guilty when his grandfather says children only look at phones, puts the phone away and asks for a story.

passage:
Sunday: At dinner, Vaibhav and his sister Rekha scrolled under the table while Dadaji talked about his old bicycle shop. Halfway through, Dadaji stopped. "Nobody hears me any more. Only phones." He went to bed early. Vaibhav's dal went cold on his plate. He felt terrible.
Monday: After school Vaibhav put a paper sign on the chai table: PHONE-FREE CHAI, 5 O'CLOCK. Rekha rolled her eyes but left her phone in the bedroom. Dadaji looked at the sign for a long time, then told them how he had fixed forty punctures in one monsoon day.
The next Sunday: At five, Dadaji was already waiting with a dusty photo album. "Today," he announced, "the story of your Dadi and the stolen mango." Vaibhav laughed so hard he snorted chai.

qa.q: What did the paper sign on the chai table say?
How did Vaibhav feel when Dadaji went to bed early?
qa.a: He felt terrible and guilty; his dal went cold.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav turn his guilt into action?
qa.a: He set up a phone-free chai time at five o'clock, which gave Dadaji people to listen.

qa.q: How did Dadaji's feelings change by the next Sunday?
qa.a: From hurt and disappointed at being ignored to eager, waiting early with the photo album.

grounding: A boy feels guilty when his grandfather says the children never talk to him because of phones, and sets up phone-free story time.
